title: Coordination of Benefit Between Two Travel Protection Certificates
content:
Where a traveller holds more than one policy of the Travel Protection Plans that answers the same incident,
the benefit is coordinated rather than duplicated: one of the two certificates is primary, and the other
answers only for what the primary did not reach.

## The rule

1. The primary policy pays to its own limit; the secondary policy pays only what remains unpaid, up to its own
   limit.
2. The primary policy is the one issued first. Where both were issued on the same day, the one with the larger
   declared trip cost is primary.
3. Benefit already consumed on a policy in this term is counted against that policy's limit whatever the claim
   type, and each claim type is additionally held to its own limit. Benefit consumed is measured over the whole
   policy term, from the issue date to the expiry or cancellation date, as the payments and the recoveries
   standing on that policy's claim record for each claim type.
4. A deductible is withheld once per claim under the primary policy and is not withheld again under the
   secondary.
5. Where the total paid across both policies would exceed the traveller's actual loss, the payment is reduced so
   that it does not, because protection indemnifies a loss and does not profit from it.
6. A recovery from a liable third party is applied first to the policy that paid last, restoring its benefit
   before the primary's.

## Ordering the two certificates

| Issue dates | Declared trip costs | Primary |
|---|---|---|
| One earlier than the other | Whatever they are | The earlier-issued certificate |
| The same day | One larger than the other | The certificate with the larger declared trip cost |

## Worked through on hypothetical figures

A loss of 4000 is answered by two certificates. The primary carries a limit of 2500 on that head and has already
consumed 500 of benefit in its term, so it pays 2000, less the deductible its plan withholds once on that claim.
The secondary carries a limit of 3000 and pays only the 2000 that remains unpaid, with no deductible withheld a
second time. Had the loss been 3500 rather than 4000, the two together would still pay no more than 3500, since
the payment is reduced to the actual loss.
